extracted.intended_audience: historians of science, bibliographers, and educated general readers interested in history of mathematics and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and critiquing historical scientific and mathematical writings (their accuracy, sourcing, editorial practice, and methodological claims), and evaluating claims about scientific method. Focuses on how to judge reliability, scholarship, and methodological virtues in historical texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on second-hand sources
rubrics_metrics.description: "writing at second-hand makes as complete mistakes about more important matters."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer primary or first-hand verification; beware that reporting second-hand can introduce complete and important errors in facts such as dates, places, and attributions. Example: Montucla's misplacement and dating of verses when relying on second-hand reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'number' and 'multitude'
rubrics_metrics.description: "an accurate distinction between _number_ and _multitude--a thing much wanted both in arithmetic and logic."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating numerical concepts, explicitly distinguish 'number' (mathematical concept) from 'multitude' (a collective or loose counting sense); failure to do so leads to confusion in arithmetic and in logical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership/admission criteria should reflect fitness not arbitrary quotas
rubrics_metrics.description: "the true intent of [the Royal Society's] charter, the true intent is, that all who are fit should be allowed to promote natural knowledge in association, from and after the time at which they are both fit and willing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional selection should be based on merit/fitness and willingness rather than fixed numerical tariffs (e.g., an arbitrary 'fifteen per annum'), which can unjustly exclude capable contributors and deviate from chartered intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid spurious numerological/superstitious justifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdote showing Councillors seeking reasons why 'fifteen' was chosen, drawing on Bungus's numerological curiosities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt numerological, mythic, or retrofitted justifications for institutional or scholarly choices; check sources and motives rather than accepting entertaining but irrelevant numerical coincidences as authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware variability and bias in personal testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: "the different colors which the same person gives to one story, according to the bias under which he tells it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat verbal recollections with caution: witness accounts may change with bias, tone, or audience. Corroborate anecdotes with other witnesses or documentary evidence; note vivid detail does not guarantee literal accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record opportunities for retraction as evidentiary fact
rubrics_metrics.description: "A time for retractation was given, both before sentence and after, which should be noted... as additional proof it gives that opinions, and opinions only, brought him to the stake."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating causes of historical punishments or condemnations, record whether opportunities for retraction were offered—this can illuminate whether action was taken for doctrinal opinion alone versus criminal conduct or other causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors and series managers are responsible for included content
rubrics_metrics.description: "This No. 87, admitted into a series, fixes upon the managers of the series, who permitted its introduction, a strong presumption of that underhand intent with which they were charged."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decisions imply responsibility: inclusion of controversial or sophistic material reflects on editors/managers and may imply tacit approval or negligence; evaluate editorial intent and oversight when judging a collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct comprehensive searches of one's holdings for completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Author's regret: "had I looked _through_ all my books, I might have made some curious additions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For bibliographical completeness or historiography, search fully through available collections (not just select items) to avoid omissions; partial searches risk missing important sources or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly transliteration/latinization practice matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism: "to Latinize the surname and not the Christian name is very unscholarlike."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt consistent and scholarly conventions when Latinizing or transliterating names; inconsistent practices can be judged unprofessional and invite criticism about accuracy and scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: No knowledge of nature without experiment and observation (empiricism first)
rubrics_metrics.description: "No knowledge of nature without experiment and observation... No derived knowledge _until_ experiment and observation are concluded."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize systematic experiment and observation before asserting derived scientific knowledge; empirical data collection is a precondition for reliable natural knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect large masses of facts and apply rules of arrangement/elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: "Bacon's ruling idea was the collection of enormous masses of facts, and then digested processes of arrangement and elimination... performs everything by the surest rules and demonstrations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt systematic gathering of extensive factual data followed by disciplined methods (classification, elimination of spurious instances) to approach scientific generalizations—i.e., methodical data aggregation plus analytic rules rather than casual induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumeratio simplex (mere enumeration) is inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: "Mere induction, _enumeratio simplex_, is spoken of by himself [Bacon] with contempt, as utterly incompetent. For Bacon knew well that a thousand instances may be contradicted by the thousand and first."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on simple enumerative induction as sufficient proof; account for potential counterexamples and use methods that provide stronger inferential warrant than simple counts of instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use methodological aids/engines to assist the intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Hooke: "The intellect is not to be suffered to act without its helps, but is continually to be assisted by some method or engine... Of this engine, no man except the incomparable Verulam [Bacon] hath had any thoughts... By this, as by that art of algebra in geometry... so will it be in the inquiry after natural knowledge."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ formal methods, tools, or 'engines' (mathematical notation, experimental apparatus, systematic protocols) to structure inquiry and reduce reliance on unaided acuteness of individual intellect; methods democratize discovery and reduce error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of refutation of fallacies (error prevention)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The part of Aristotle's logic of which he saw the value was the book on _refutation of fallacies_." and characterization of Bacon as "eminently the philosopher of _error prevented_, not of _progress facilitated_."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give explicit attention to identifying and refuting fallacies and sources of error as a core component of sound inquiry; preventing error is a distinct and valuable contribution to reliable progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate facts from laws; deduce laws only after facts are settled
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wait, says Bacon, until the facts are determined: ... Wait, says Bacon, until all the facts, or all the obtainable facts, are brought in: apply my rules of separation to the facts, and the result shall come out as easily as by ruler and compasses."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In scientific evaluation, first collect and settle empirical facts, apply rigorous methods to separate genuine signals from noise and error, and only then infer general laws; avoid premature theorizing from incomplete data.
